items: Bytes go ==straight to the block store== via presigned URLs, never through app servers
Chunks the server already has are skipped, so an edit uploads only the changed chunks
Nothing is visible to other devices until ==commit== succeeds
Upload session = `upload_id` + ==bitmap of received chunks==, kept for **7 days**
Drop after **600 of 1000** chunks: resume sends only the remaining ==400==
Per-chunk retry with ==exponential backoff==, **3 tries**, then the session stays resumable
Manifest = ordered hash list plus signed CDN URLs
==Range requests== give streaming and partial reads
==Commit rejects== if any listed chunk is not present
So a version **never points at a missing block**

sections.title: Sync Engine and Conflict Resolution (Cloud File Storage)

pages.title: Sync Engine and Conflict Resolution (Cloud File Storage)

items: Goal: ==converge== every device to the same tree
Each device stores a ==cursor== = last change-log `seq` it applied
Sync = **pull** `GET /changes?cursor=N`, apply locally, **push** local edits via commit
Server keeps a per-namespace ==append-only change log==: (file_id, version, op, seq)
Client compares **local hash list vs remote**, transfers only differing chunks
Offline edits **queue** locally and replay on reconnect, each with its base_version
Every commit carries ==base_version== (the version the edit started from)
Server's `latest_version` != base_version means two devices edited the same base
Optimistic check (or version vector): **never** a silent overwrite

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Ordering edits by device **wall-clock time** (last-writer-wins) silently loses data. Order by the server's ==version== and keep the loser as a conflicted copy.

items: Goal: keep ==history== so any mistake can be undone
Each commit adds a new **immutable** version row
The row points at a ==block list== (ordered chunk hashes)
Unchanged chunks are **shared** between versions
Delete = ==soft delete== flag; file moves to trash, nothing freed yet
Cap: **100 versions per file**, applied only past day 30
Expired version row decrements its chunk refcounts
Restore creates a ==new head version== with the old block list
**No bytes copied**: one metadata write
History stays intact; the restore is itself a version

items: {green:Metadata}: shard by ==namespace_id==, 64 to 1K shards, 1 primary + 2 replicas each

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Bytes go to the ==block store==, truth lives in ==metadata==. Versions are server-assigned, blocks are immutable, and a block is deleted only after two checks.

blocks.q: A GC job deletes any chunk whose refcount is 0. A 50 GB upload has sent 600 of 1000 chunks, and the commit has not happened yet. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
a_bullets: The 600 uploaded chunks have ==refcount 0==, because no committed version points at them yet
GC deletes them, so the resume finds them gone, or the commit is rejected because listed chunks are missing
Fix: delete only after a ==grace period==, which is the 7-day upload session expiry
Also require two checks before deleting: refcount is 0 and no live manifest or session references the chunk

blocks.q: Phone and laptop both hold version 5 of report.docx. The laptop commits with base_version=5. Later the offline phone commits its own edit with base_version=5. What does the server do?
a_bullets: The laptop's commit succeeds, so latest_version becomes 6
The phone's commit has latest_version 6 != base_version 5, so the optimistic check fails
Nothing is overwritten: the phone's edit is saved as a ==conflicted copy== next to the original
The check uses server-assigned versions, not wall-clock time, so clock skew on the phone cannot change the outcome

blocks.q: The client uses fixed 4 MB chunks on a 1 GB file (256 chunks). Case A: one byte in the middle is overwritten. Case B: one byte is inserted at the very start. How much is uploaded in each case?
a_bullets: Case A: only the one chunk containing that byte changes, so about ==4 MB== is uploaded
Case B: every byte shifts by 1, so all 256 chunk boundaries and hashes change, and about ==1 GB== is uploaded
Content-defined chunking (rolling hash) places boundaries by content, so an insert changes only the chunks near it
The trade-off is that content-defined chunking is more complex than fixed chunking

blocks.q: Alice revokes Bob's access to a shared folder. The permission cache TTL is 60 s and block URLs are signed for 5 min. What is the worst case before Bob is fully locked out?
a_bullets: For up to ==60 s== the stale cache can still say Bob is allowed, so he can still be issued a new block URL
A URL issued at the last moment stays valid for ==5 min==
Worst case is about 6 minutes: revocation takes effect within minutes, not instantly
A permanent public URL would never expire, which is why block URLs are short-lived and signed

blocks.q: A notifier server crashes, so its devices miss the push saying namespace 42 reached seq 900. Is data lost, and how do the devices recover?
a_bullets: No data is lost: the push carries only {namespace_id, seq}, and the real changes live in the change log
Each client polls /changes every 5 min as a fallback, using its stored cursor
The pull is idempotent, so the device fetches everything after its cursor and ends up at seq 900
Reconnecting devices use jittered backoff so they do not all hit the notifiers at once
